User: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $22,100 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $920 interest from Marcus savings account and $195 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $2,700 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $800 to Doctors Without Borders have the receipt, and had $650 in work sup

plies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Thanks — I can walk you through what’s deductible, which deduction method will likely win, how to treat the home office, and which forms/worksheets you’ll use. I’ll show approximate numbers so you can see the tax impact.

Quick summary up front
- You should report the $22,100 consulting as self‑employment income on Schedule C and pay self‑employment (SE) tax (Schedule SE). That also lets you

deduct business expenses (the $650 supplies and a home office deduction).  
- The $920 interest and $195 dividends are taxable and reported on Form 1040.  
- Student loan interest (you paid $2,700) is an above‑the‑line deduction (up to $2,500 allowed; subject to income limits). Based on the numbers you gave, you should be under the AGI phaseout and able to claim this deduction (I’ll show estimates).  
- Your $800 cash gift to Doctors Without Borders is an itemized charitable deduction (you need/should keep

the receipt/acknowledgement).  
- For 2023 the standard deduction for Married Filing Jointly is $27,700 — with only $800 in charitable contributions (and no other itemizable items given), you will almost certainly take the standard deduction on your federal return.  
- The home office deduction (for the portion used by your consulting/self‑employed work) is available and will reduce your Schedule C net profit whether or not you itemize. You can choose the simplified method ($5/sq ft) or the actual method (u

se Form 8829); the actual method looks considerably more favorable given your rent and office size — but it requires exclusive/regular use and supporting records.

Details, calculations, and recommendations

1) What to report and where
- W-2 wages ($84,900): Form 1040, wages line (and attached W-2).  
- Consulting income ($22,100): Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business). On Schedule C you deduct business expenses (supplies, home office deduction, etc.) to get net profit.  
- Self-employment tax: Schedule

SE (you pay SE tax on net earnings from self‑employment). Half of SE tax is deductible as an adjustment on Schedule 1 (reduces AGI).  
- Interest ($920) and dividends ($195): reported on Form 1040 (and potentially 1099‑INT/1099‑DIV if issued).  
- Student loan interest ($2,700): claimed on Schedule 1, adjustment to income (up to $2,500 allowed if your MAGI is under the phaseout).  
- Charitable gift ($800): Schedule A (itemize) — but see the standard vs itemize section below.
- Home office: either Form 882

9 (actual method) attached to Schedule C, or simplified method (enter the simplified deduction amount on Schedule C).

2) Home office — eligibility & method
Eligibility rules (key points)
- You must use the 165 sq ft space regularly and exclusively for business (no personal use of that room).  
- The office must be your principal place of business for the consulting work (or used to meet clients, etc.).  
If these are true, you can claim a home office deduction for the self‑employment portion only.

Two met

hods
A. Simplified method
- $5 per square foot up to 300 sq ft.  
- For 165 sq ft: 165 × $5 = $825 deduction. No Form 8829; easier recordkeeping.

B. Actual method (Form 8829)
- Allocate direct and indirect home expenses by the business percentage. Business percentage = office sq ft / total home sq ft = 165 / 690 = 23.91% (≈23.9%).  
- Rent: $2,050 × 12 = $24,600 per year. Business portion of rent ≈ 24,600 × 23.91% ≈ $5,882. Plus you may allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs, etc., proportionally.

Use Form 8829 to compute allowable deduction.
- Actual method typically gives a much larger deduction here (assuming the room is exclusive/business only and you have records).

Which to choose?
- If the office truly is exclusive and regular, the actual method will be more beneficial given your rent, and it reduces your Schedule C net profit substantially. If you can’t meet exclusive use or you want simplicity, use simplified.

3) Rough numbers (two scenarios) — to show impact on AGI and student loan intere

st phaseout
Scenario A — Actual home office (use rent allocation only for simplicity)
- Consulting gross: 22,100
- Supplies: 650
- Home office (actual portion of rent only): ≈ 5,882
- Net profit (Schedule C) ≈ 22,100 − 650 − 5,882 = 15,568
- SE tax: calculation uses 92.35% × net profit = 0.9235×15,568 ≈ 14,378 taxable amount; SE tax ≈ 15.3%×14,378 ≈ $2,199
- Deductible half SE tax (above the line) ≈ $1,099
- AGI estimate: W-2 84,900 + net SE 15,568 = 100,468; subtract half SE tax 1,099 and student loan inte

rest 2,500 (limit) or 2,500 if phaseout — you paid 2,700 but max deductible is $2,500; actually if your MAGI is under phaseout you can deduct up to $2,500. So AGI ≈ 100,468 − 1,099 − 2,500 = 96,869 (note: I used $2,500 cap — see note below).

Important note about student loan interest: the maximum deduction is $2,500 per return. Although you paid $2,700, only up to $2,500 is allowed on the federal return. (If your MAGI exceeds the phaseout, the deduction phases out completely above the upper limit.) Based o

n these numbers your MAGI is well below the $145k MFJ phaseout start for 2023, so you should be able to take the full $2,500 cap.

Scenario B — Simplified home office
- Consulting gross: 22,100
- Supplies: 650
- Home office simplified: 825
- Net profit ≈ 22,100 − 650 − 825 = 20,625
- SE tax: 0.9235×20,625 ≈ 19,057 → SE tax ≈ 2,917; half SE tax ≈ 1,459
- AGI estimate: 84,900 + 20,625 − 1,459 − 2,500 = 101,566

Conclusion from scenarios:
- The actual home office method produces a larger Schedule C deduction a

nd lowers AGI more than the simplified method. It also lowers the SE tax base. If you meet exclusive/regular use and can substantiate the allocation, the actual method appears more beneficial.

4) Standard deduction vs. itemizing
- 2023 MFJ standard deduction = $27,700.
- You told me of $800 charitable contributions only (plus maybe state income taxes paid when filing, but you didn’t list state tax payments or mortgage interest or property tax). With only $800 in charitable donations and no other large item

ized items you will almost certainly use the standard deduction.
- Taking the home office deduction is separate: even if you take the standard deduction on Schedule A, your home office deduction still reduces your Schedule C net profit (so you benefit from it whether or not you itemize).

5) Specific forms / worksheets to use
- Federal:
  - Form 1040 (main return)
  - Schedule 1 — adjustments to income (student loan interest is reported here; half SE tax is an adjustment shown on Schedule 1)
  - Schedule C

— profit or loss from business (report $22,100 revenue, $650 supplies, home office deduction or attach Form 8829)
  - Schedule SE — self‑employment tax calculation
  - Form 8829 — if you use the actual method for the home office (computes allowable portion of rent, utilities, etc.). If you use the simplified method, do not file Form 8829 — instead report the simplified amount on Schedule C.
  - Schedule A — only if you itemize (seems unlikely given standard deduction).
  - Form 1040-ES — for quarterly estim

ated payments if you owe estimated tax during the year (to avoid penalties).
- Oregon state:
  - Oregon Form OR‑40 (for residents) — Oregon starts from federal AGI with state adjustments; you’ll report your federal AGI and then make state-specific adjustments. You’ll also pay state income tax on your income; keep in mind Oregon tax is separate from federal. (If you made estimated tax payments to Oregon you’ll report them when you file OR‑40.)

6) Records to keep
- Bank records or 1099s showing consulting in

come (clients may issue 1099‑NEC if they paid $600+). Keep all invoices and receipts.  
- Receipts for the $800 charitable gift (required for cash contributions over $250 — you said you have a receipt).  
- Student loan interest statement (Form 1098‑E) or lender statements for $2,700 interest paid.  
- Rent receipts, utility bills, photos/floorplan and documentation proving exclusive/regular use of the 165 sq ft office if you claim the home office actual method.  
- Records of supplies, business mileage (if

any), and other business expenses.

7) Other items & planning suggestions
- You likely must pay self‑employment tax (Schedule SE) and possibly quarterly estimated taxes. If you haven’t been paying estimated taxes, you may owe a tax bill when you file; consider making estimated payments next year or adjusting withholding on the W‑2 spouse (if applicable).  
- You may be able to contribute to a SEP IRA or solo 401(k) to reduce taxable income — consider this if you want to lower taxes and save for retirement.

- Make sure the home office is truly used exclusively for the business; the IRS is strict about exclusive use. If the room doubles as a guest room, you cannot claim the home office deduction for that space.

8) Final recommendation for your situation
- Use Schedule C for the $22,100 consulting income. Claim the $650 supplies on Schedule C.  
- If your 165 sq ft office is used exclusively and regularly for business, use the actual home office method (Form 8829) — it looks more favorable given your rent. I

f you can’t substantiate exclusive use or prefer simplicity, use the simplified method ($825). Either method reduces your Schedule C net profit.  
- Take the standard deduction on your federal return (MFJ $27,700) rather than itemizing, since your only reported itemizable amount is $800 charity (unless you have other state taxes, mortgage interest, large medical expenses, etc., not listed).  
- Claim student loan interest up to the $2,500 cap on Schedule 1 (you paid $2,700 but the federal cap is $2,500; you

should be under the MAGI phaseout based on your numbers).

If you’d like, I can:
- Prepare a step‑by‑step checklist for filling in each form (Schedule C line by line with the numbers), or
- Run through exact calculations using either home office method and show estimated federal tax owed/refund (I’d need to know any other deductions, state tax withheld, estimated payments, retirement contributions, etc.), or
- Draft a list of documents you should gather for tax prep and what to give to your tax preparer.
Which of those would you like next?
